title: The luminous mysteries
hook: added by John Paul II in 2002: baptism, Cana, the kingdom, transfiguration, Eucharist (Thursdays)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the joyful mysteries, and the word mystery: a hidden thing opened up. Your line was joy has a story.

Picture the whole Gospel laid out on a table, and the rosary's mysteries as pins stuck into it. For a long time there were fifteen. Five joyful: the birth and childhood of Jesus. Five sorrowful: his suffering and death. Five glorious: the resurrection and after. There's a big empty stretch in the middle. Jesus is twelve in the Temple, and the very next pin is the night before he dies. Everything in between, the baptism, the miracles, the parables, the crowds, is missing. Then in October 2002, a pope who had prayed the rosary since he was young added five.
screen: `FIFTEEN MYSTERIES.` → `A GAP IN THE MIDDLE.` → `2002: A POPE ADDS FIVE.`

segments.voice: Pope John Paul the Second called them the mysteries of light, in Latin mysteria lucis. Luminous means full of light. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." These five cover his public life, when that light was out in the open. First, the Baptism in the Jordan: Jesus goes down into the water, the heavens open, and a voice calls him the beloved Son. Second, the Wedding at Cana: the wine runs out, and Mary tells the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Water becomes wine, his first sign. Third, the Proclamation of the Kingdom: the preaching, the call to turn around, the forgiveness. Fourth, the Transfiguration: on a mountain, his face shines like the sun in front of three friends. Fifth, the Institution of the Eucharist: the Last Supper, the bread and cup you met at the consecration last week. The baptism, Cana and the mountain were all stories in Camp Two; now they're beads. The Pope suggested praying them on Thursdays, the day of the Last Supper, and moved the joyful mysteries to Saturday to make room. He said plainly the addition was offered freely, not imposed. Some Catholics pray all twenty. Some keep the traditional fifteen. Both are at home in the Church. The gap is filled: the rosary now walks through the whole life, including the years when the light was out on the road.
screen: `MYSTERIA LUCIS: MYSTERIES OF LIGHT.` · `JORDAN, CANA, THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MOUNTAIN, THE SUPPER.` · `OFFERED FREELY, NOT IMPOSED.` · then, large: `I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Pick one scene, the river, the wedding running out of wine, the crowds, the mountain, the supper, and put yourself inside it; at Cana, maybe you're a servant, told to fill jars with water and not sure why. If you pray, begin a luminous decade on your fingers, and let the scene play. If you don't, stay with the picture, and notice where the light falls.
Luminous mysteries. Five scenes of light from Jesus's public life, added to the rosary in 2002 and prayed on Thursdays. Today's word.
Your line: the light years. Thursday now has five scenes of its own. That's day one hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Catholics who use them pray the luminous mysteries of the rosary on Thursdays, meditating on the Baptism of Jesus, the Wedding at Cana, the Proclamation of the Kingdom, the Transfiguration and the Institution of the Eucharist; some keep the traditional fifteen mysteries.

notes: Douay-Rheims John 8:12 and John 2:5 given from memory; confirm.

Rosarium Virginis Mariae (October 16, 2002): RVM 19 presents the addition as left to the freedom of individuals and communities; RVM 38 moves the joyful mysteries to Saturday and puts the luminous on Thursday. Confirm.
'For over four hundred years, fifteen mysteries': since Pius V (1569). Confirm.
Camp Two references: the baptism (day 32), Cana (day 35), the mountain (day 52); the consecration was day 114.
Both the traditional fifteen and the twenty are described without ranking.
